newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal, India sign landmark power trade agreement.
newsitem.headline: Nepal, India sign landmark power trade agreement.

text.p: Nepal and India signed a pathbreaking agreement on Thursday allowing private firms from both nations to produce and trade electric power, Nepali and Indian officials said.

They said visiting Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Nepali counterpart, Lokendra Bahadur Chand, were present as their junior ministers signed the agreement. Previously, only the governments of both nations could trade electricity.
"It is believed that the agreement will attract private funds in Nepal's water resources development and contribute to the country's economic growth," a Nepali government statement said.
Gujral, the first foreign leader to visit the Himalayan kingdom since Chand took office in March, arrived in Kathmandu on Thursday on a three-day official visit.
After his arrival, the two neighbours exchanged instruments of ratification that made effective a 1996 water-sharing treaty, which ended a dispute that had soured bilateral ties for years.
"We have been able to discuss every issue and we have agreed on every issue," Gujral told reporters after an hour-long discussion with Chand. He did not elaborate.

The tiny Himalayan kingdom's water-sharing accords with its giant southern neighbour have been a prickly political issue since Nepal agreed to two river projects in the 1950s that critics said favoured India.

Nepal's parliament had repeatedly criticised the government five years ago for leasing land to India for a dam being built by New Delhi in 1991 at Tanakpur town on the Mahakali river, along their border.
The 1996 treaty established the principle of equality in the division of Mahakali water.
Gujral said a joint boundary team had been asked to settle a dispute regarding the origin of the Mahakali within one month.
The treaty also defined terms for a $5 billion dam on the river at Pancheswar, upstream from Tanakpur, to generate 6,400 megawatts of power that the two nations would share equally.
Nepal, which possesses the potential to produce 83,000 megawatts of hydroelectric power, generates only 293 megawatts against a peak demand of 302 megawatts.

Under the pact, Kathmandu can sell most of its share of electricity from the new plant to power-starved India. Nepali officials hope the pact will help trim the kingdom's $380.7 million trade deficit with India.
The communist opposition in 1996 complained the treaty would not balance the distribution of water from two existing projects on the river, the Tanakpur dam and the Sarada barrage.

They eventually relented and supported the treaty during a parliamentary ratification last September after Nepal and India promised to consider their concerns in a detailed project report, due by December 1997.
The communists now dominate Chand's two-month-old coalition government.
Nepal and India also signed three other agreements for cooperation on civil aviation, health and transportation.

As foreign minister in 1990, Gujral helped end a deadlock in relations over the kingdom's transit facilities through India, which had closed down extra entry points used by Nepali traders for 15 months.

Land-locked Nepal is now pressing its southern neighbour for permission to use a 71-km (44 mile) route across India to give its traders easy access to the Bangladesh port of Chittagong, as an alternative outlet to the sea.

Negotiators said Gujral had refused any role for India in a dispute between Nepal and the neighbouring kingdom of Bhutan over the return of 90,000 refugees of ethnic Nepali origin from Bhutan. They said Gujral had urged them to resolve the problem bilaterally.
